intro: Today you learn to make one part of a word strong, like TEA-cher and ho-TEL, and to finish words with two consonants at the end, like desk and lunch. You also learn to find the stress of any word in a dictionary. Listen, copy and say every word out loud!
teachingNotes: Explain 'stress' in plain words the first time: one syllable (one beat) of the word is louder, longer and a little higher; the other syllables are short and quiet. Indonesian has no strong word stress (syllables sound almost equally strong), so learners say English words flat or copy the Indonesian word: hotel, gitar, Juli become HO-tel, GI-tar, JU-li. In English they are ho-TEL, gui-TAR, Ju-LY. Use CAPITALS for the stressed syllable (TEA-cher); never bare IPA.

Common errors from the node: hotel said as HO-tel (right: ho-TEL), teacher said as tea-CHER (right: TEA-cher). Give the A1 rule of thumb: most two-syllable nouns stress the FIRST syllable (TEA-cher, DOC-tor, WA-ter, MOR-ning, OF-fice). Name the exceptions as a short list to remember: loanwords like hotel, guitar, police, July, machine; words starting with a weak a-, be- or to- (a-GAIN, be-HIND, to-DAY, to-NIGHT); longer words like ba-NA-na, com-PU-ter. Numbers: four-TEEN vs FOR-ty (the -teen numbers are stressed on -TEEN when said alone or at the end of a sentence).

Final consonants: Indonesian words almost never end with two consonants, so learners drop one ('des' for desk, 'mil' for milk, 'tes' for test, 'frien' for friend) or add a vowel ('deske'). Say the whole ending: desk = s then k; lunch ends like the 'c' of Indonesian 'cari' (LANCH); box ends with 'ks'. Show why it matters: card without d is car, tent without t is ten, belt without t is bell. Linking tip: before a vowel the last consonant joins the next word (my desk is → 'my des-kis').

Dictionary stress: in Cambridge, Oxford and Longman (free online and in apps) the pronunciation is between slashes, e.g. hotel /həʊˈtel/. The learner does NOT need to read every symbol: find the small high mark ˈ; the syllable right AFTER it is stressed. Dots (.) show where syllables split. A low mark ˌ (fifteen /ˌfɪfˈtiːn/) is a weaker stress: ignore it for now. Press the UK or US speaker button and copy. Some other dictionaries put the mark after the syllable or print it in bold: check the guide at the front.

British vs American: stress is almost always the same; a few words differ, e.g. address (UK a-DRESS, US often AD-dress). Accept both. Unstressed syllables often become a weak 'uh' (TEA-chuh in British English), but don't drill vowel reduction beyond that.

Stay in scope: only grammar the learner knows (be, simple present, there is, have got, can, short questions). No past simple (except was/were), no future forms, no perfect tenses, no comparatives. Don't teach sentence stress, secondary stress rules or stress-shift rules for word families (PHO-to / pho-TO-gra-pher).

keyPoints.title: Make one syllable strong
keyPoints.explanation: A syllable is one beat of a word (ma-kan has 2). In English one syllable is stressed: louder, longer and higher. Most two-syllable nouns stress the first syllable: TEA-cher, DOC-tor, WA-ter. Learn the exceptions: ho-TEL, gui-TAR, Ju-LY, a-GAIN, to-DAY, be-HIND, com-PU-ter, and -teen numbers (four-TEEN, but FOR-ty).

examples.en: The hotel is near the station.

id.title: Buat satu suku kata kuat
id.explanation: Suku kata = satu ketukan dalam kata (ma-kan punya 2). Dalam bahasa Inggris, satu suku kata diberi tekanan: lebih keras, lebih panjang dan lebih tinggi. Kebanyakan kata benda dua suku kata ditekan di suku kata pertama: TEA-cher, DOC-tor, WA-ter. Hafalkan pengecualiannya: ho-TEL, gui-TAR, Ju-LY, a-GAIN, to-DAY, be-HIND, com-PU-ter, dan angka -teen (four-TEEN, tapi FOR-ty).

keyPoints.title: Finish the word: desk, lunch
keyPoints.explanation: Many English words end with two consonants together: desk, milk, test, hand, lunch. Say all of them, and don't add a vowel after them. If you drop the last sound, the word can change: card becomes car, tent becomes ten.

examples.en: My phone is on the desk.
examples.id: HP-ku ada di atas meja. (desk: s + k)
Kami makan siang jam dua belas. (lunch: akhirnya seperti 'c' di cari)
Boleh saya bayar pakai kartu? (card, bukan car)

id.title: Selesaikan katanya: desk, lunch
id.explanation: Banyak kata bahasa Inggris berakhir dengan dua konsonan sekaligus: desk, milk, test, hand, lunch. Ucapkan semuanya, dan jangan tambahkan vokal sesudahnya. Kalau bunyi terakhir hilang, katanya bisa berubah: card jadi car, tent jadi ten.

keyPoints.title: Find the stress in a dictionary
keyPoints.explanation: In an online dictionary (Cambridge, Oxford, Longman), look at the pronunciation between slashes. Find the small high mark ˈ: the syllable right after it is stressed. hotel /həʊˈtel/ = ho-TEL. Then press the speaker button and copy.

id.title: Cari tekanan kata di kamus
id.explanation: Di kamus online (Cambridge, Oxford, Longman), lihat cara baca di antara dua garis miring. Cari tanda kecil di atas ˈ: suku kata tepat sesudahnya yang ditekan. hotel /həʊˈtel/ = ho-TEL. Lalu tekan tombol speaker dan tirukan.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which syllable is stressed in 'teacher': first or second?
guidedPractice.hint: Most two-syllable nouns are strong at the start: TEA-cher.

guidedPractice.prompt: Which word is stressed on the second syllable: water, today or morning? Write it.
guidedPractice.hint: Words that start with a weak to-, a- or be- are strong later: to-DAY.

guidedPractice.prompt: Sari says: 'I drink mil every morning.' Which sound is missing at the end of 'milk'? Write the letter.
guidedPractice.hint: milk ends with two consonants: l and then k. Say both.

guidedPractice.prompt: A dictionary shows hotel /həʊˈtel/. The mark ˈ is before 'tel'. Which syllable is stressed: first or second?
guidedPractice.hint: The syllable right after the high mark ˈ is the strong one: ho-TEL.

independentPractice.prompt: Write first or second: where is the stress in 'guitar'?
independentPractice.hint: In Indonesian it's 'gitar', but in English it's gui-TAR.

independentPractice.prompt: Write the English word for 'ujian'. Then say it with a clear -st at the end.
independentPractice.hint: Not 'tes': finish with s and then t.

independentPractice.prompt: A dictionary shows breakfast /ˈbrek.fəst/. Which syllable is stressed: first or second?
independentPractice.hint: The mark ˈ is at the very start, before 'brek': BREAK-fast.

assessment.prompt: Choose the correct answer. Which word is stressed on the FIRST syllable: hotel, kitchen or again? Choose it.
assessment.rubric: Correct: kitchen (KIT-chen, a two-syllable noun stressed at the start). 'hotel' (ho-TEL) and 'again' (a-GAIN) are stressed on the second syllable = 0.

assessment.prompt: Choose the correct answer. Listen. Choose the number you hear.
assessment.rubric: Correct: 70 (SEV-en-ty, stress at the start). '17' = 0: seventeen is stressed at the end (seven-TEEN). Spelling slip like 'seventi' = 50.

assessment.prompt: Choose the correct answer. Listen. Do you hear six or sick? Choose the word you hear.
assessment.rubric: Correct: six (ends with 'ks'). Accept '6'. 'sick' = 0: the final s was heard.

assessment.prompt: Choose the correct answer. Budi says: 'This is my frien, Dimas.' Which sound is missing at the end of 'friend'? Choose the letter.
assessment.rubric: Correct: d (friend ends with n + d). 'n' = 0 (Budi said the n). 'nd' = 50.

assessment.prompt: Choose the correct answer. A dictionary shows potato /pəˈteɪ.təʊ/. Which syllable is stressed: first, second or third? Choose it.
assessment.rubric: Correct: second (po-TA-to: the mark ˈ comes right before 'teɪ'). 'first' or 'third' = 0.

assessment.prompt: Choose the correct answer. In the Cambridge and Oxford dictionaries, does the stress mark ˈ come before or after the stressed syllable? Choose before or after.
assessment.rubric: Correct: before (hotel /həʊˈtel/: the mark is before 'tel'). 'after' = 0.
options: at the end of the word

blocks.text:
A **syllable** is one beat of a word: *ma-kan* has 2 beats, *bus* has 1, *teach-er* has 2. In English, words with two or more syllables have **one strong syllable**. We call it the **stress**. The stressed syllable is:
- **louder**,
- **longer**,
- a little **higher**.
The other syllables are short and quiet, often just a weak 'uh': *teacher* sounds like **TEE-chuh** in British English.

In this lesson we write the stressed syllable in CAPITALS: **TEA-cher**, **DOC-tor**.

**The Indonesian trap:** Indonesian has no strong stress. The syllables of *guru* or *dokter* sound almost equally strong. So many learners say English words flat, or put the stress at the end: *tea-CHER*. People may not understand you, even if every sound is right.

id.text:
**Suku kata** = satu ketukan dalam kata: *ma-kan* punya 2 ketukan, *bus* punya 1, *teach-er* punya 2. Dalam bahasa Inggris, kata yang punya dua suku kata atau lebih punya **satu suku kata yang kuat**. Itu disebut **tekanan** (stress). Suku kata yang ditekan itu:
- **lebih keras**,
- **lebih panjang**,
- sedikit **lebih tinggi** nadanya.
Suku kata lainnya pendek dan pelan, sering hanya bunyi 'e' lemah seperti di *kelas*: *teacher* terdengar seperti **TII-che** dalam bahasa Inggris British.

Di pelajaran ini suku kata yang ditekan ditulis dengan HURUF BESAR: **TEA-cher**, **DOC-tor**.

**Jebakan bahasa Indonesia:** bahasa Indonesia tidak punya tekanan yang kuat. Suku kata di *guru* atau *dokter* terdengar hampir sama kuat. Jadi banyak pelajar mengucapkan kata bahasa Inggris datar saja, atau menekan bagian akhirnya: *tea-CHER*. Orang bisa tidak paham, walaupun setiap bunyinya sudah benar.

blocks.text: Rule of thumb: **most two-syllable nouns** (names of people, places and things) are stressed on the **first** syllable. Clap once loudly and once softly: CLAP-clap = TEA-cher.

id.text: Pegangan praktis: **kebanyakan kata benda dua suku kata** (nama orang, tempat dan benda) ditekan di suku kata **pertama**. Tepuk tangan sekali keras dan sekali pelan: PLOK-plok = TEA-cher.

blocks.explain: teacher is a two-syllable noun, so the first syllable is strong: TEA-cher. tea-CHER is a very common mistake.

id.explain: teacher adalah kata benda dua suku kata, jadi suku kata pertama yang kuat: TEA-cher. tea-CHER adalah kesalahan yang sangat umum.

material.title: Why is it ho-TEL and not HO-tel?

blocks.text:
Some common words don't follow the rule of thumb. They are stressed **later**. There is no simple rule for all of them, so learn this short list:
- **Words from other languages**, many of them also in Indonesian: *hotel* → **ho-TEL**, *guitar* → **gui-TAR**, *police* → **po-LICE**, *machine* → **ma-CHINE**, *July* → **Ju-LY**. In Indonesian we say *HO-tel*, *GI-tar*, *JU-li*, so these are the words we get wrong most often.
- **Words that start with a weak a-, be- or to-**: **a-GAIN**, **a-BOUT**, **be-HIND**, **be-TWEEN**, **to-DAY**, **to-NIGHT**. The first syllable is only a quick 'uh' or 'bi'.
- **Some longer words**: **ba-NA-na**, **com-PU-ter**, **In-do-NE-sia** (4 syllables in English, 5 in Indonesian!).
- **Numbers**: the -teen numbers are strong at the end, the -ty numbers at the start: **four-TEEN** (14) but **FOR-ty** (40), **six-TEEN** (16) but **SIX-ty** (60). That's how people hear the difference.

British and American English almost always stress words the same way. A few words differ: *address* is **a-DRESS** in British English and often **AD-dress** in American English. Both are correct.

id.text:
Beberapa kata umum tidak mengikuti pegangan tadi. Tekanannya ada **di belakang**. Tidak ada satu aturan sederhana untuk semuanya, jadi hafalkan daftar pendek ini:
- **Kata serapan dari bahasa lain**, banyak juga ada di bahasa Indonesia: *hotel* → **ho-TEL**, *guitar* → **gui-TAR**, *police* → **po-LICE**, *machine* → **ma-CHINE**, *July* → **Ju-LY**. Dalam bahasa Indonesia kita bilang *HO-tel*, *GI-tar*, *JU-li*, jadi kata-kata inilah yang paling sering salah.
- **Kata yang diawali a-, be- atau to- yang lemah**: **a-GAIN**, **a-BOUT**, **be-HIND**, **be-TWEEN**, **to-DAY**, **to-NIGHT**. Suku kata pertamanya hanya 'e' atau 'bi' yang cepat.
- **Beberapa kata yang lebih panjang**: **ba-NA-na**, **com-PU-ter**, **In-do-NE-sia** (4 suku kata dalam bahasa Inggris, 5 dalam bahasa Indonesia!).
- **Angka**: angka -teen kuat di akhir, angka -ty kuat di awal: **four-TEEN** (14) tapi **FOR-ty** (40), **six-TEEN** (16) tapi **SIX-ty** (60). Dari situlah orang mendengar bedanya.

Bahasa Inggris British dan Amerika hampir selalu memberi tekanan yang sama. Ada beberapa kata yang berbeda: *address* (alamat) dibaca **a-DRESS** dalam bahasa Inggris British dan sering **AD-dress** dalam bahasa Inggris Amerika. Keduanya benar.

rows.en: The hotel is near the station.
The bank is behind the mosque.

blocks.text: When a word looks like an Indonesian word (hotel, gitar, polisi, mesin, Juli), be careful: the English stress is often at the **end**. If you're not sure, check it in a dictionary (see the last section).

id.text: Kalau sebuah kata mirip kata Indonesia (hotel, gitar, polisi, mesin, Juli), hati-hati: tekanan bahasa Inggrisnya sering ada di **akhir**. Kalau ragu, cek di kamus (lihat bagian terakhir).

blocks.prompt: Which word is stressed like ho-TEL (on the second syllable)?
blocks.explain: behind starts with a weak be-, so the second syllable is strong: be-HIND. office (OF-fice) and water (WA-ter) are nouns stressed on the first syllable.

id.prompt: Kata mana yang tekanannya seperti ho-TEL (di suku kata kedua)?
id.explain: behind diawali be- yang lemah, jadi suku kata kedua yang kuat: be-HIND. office (OF-fice) dan water (WA-ter) adalah kata benda yang ditekan di suku kata pertama.

blocks.text:
In A0 you learnt to finish every word: *cat*, *bed*, *bus*. Many English words end with **two consonants together** (a **consonant** is a 'huruf mati' sound like k, s, t, d, n, l). Indonesian words almost never end like that, so two mistakes are very common:
- **dropping the last sound**: *desk* → 'des', *milk* → 'mil', *test* → 'tes', *hand* → 'han';
- **adding a vowel**: *desk* → 'deske', *milk* → 'milek'.

Why does it matter? Without the last sound, it can become a different word: *card* → **car** (kartu → mobil), *tent* → **ten**, *belt* → **bell**.

How to say them:
- **desk**: say *des*, then close with a light **k**.
- **lunch**: it ends like the **c** of *cari*: 'LANCH'. Don't stop at 'lan'.
- **box**: the x is two sounds, **k + s**: 'boks'.

id.text:
Di A0 kamu sudah belajar menyelesaikan setiap kata: *cat*, *bed*, *bus*. Banyak kata bahasa Inggris berakhir dengan **dua konsonan sekaligus** (**konsonan** = huruf mati seperti k, s, t, d, n, l). Kata bahasa Indonesia hampir tidak pernah berakhir seperti itu, jadi ada dua kesalahan yang sangat umum:
- **menghilangkan bunyi terakhir**: *desk* → 'des', *milk* → 'mil', *test* → 'tes', *hand* → 'han';
- **menambah vokal**: *desk* → 'deske', *milk* → 'milek'.

Kenapa penting? Tanpa bunyi terakhir, katanya bisa berubah: *card* → **car** (kartu → mobil), *tent* → **ten** (tenda → sepuluh), *belt* → **bell** (sabuk → bel).

Cara mengucapkannya:
- **desk**: ucapkan *des*, lalu tutup dengan **k** yang ringan.
- **lunch**: akhirnya seperti **c** di *cari*: 'LANC'. Jangan berhenti di 'lan'.
- **box**: huruf x itu dua bunyi, **k + s**: 'boks'.

blocks.text: Hard to say? Go slowly first: *des... k*, then faster: *desk*. And when the next word starts with a vowel, move the last sound over: *my desk is* → 'my des-kis', *a hand on* → 'a han-don'. It's easier and sounds natural.

id.text: Sulit diucapkan? Pelan-pelan dulu: *des... k*, lalu lebih cepat: *desk*. Dan kalau kata berikutnya diawali vokal, sambungkan bunyi terakhirnya ke kata itu: *my desk is* → 'my des-kis', *a hand on* → 'a han-don'. Lebih mudah dan terdengar alami.

blocks.prompt: Rina wants to pay with her bank card, but she says 'Can I pay by car?' Which sound did she drop?
blocks.explain: card ends with a d. Without the d, people hear car (mobil). Finish the word: car-d.

id.prompt: Rina mau bayar pakai kartu bank, tapi dia bilang 'Can I pay by car?' Bunyi apa yang dia hilangkan?
id.explain: card berakhir dengan d. Tanpa d, orang mendengar car (mobil). Selesaikan katanya: car-d.

material.title: Check the stress in a dictionary

blocks.text:
Not sure where the stress is? A good English dictionary tells you. Free online dictionaries like **Cambridge**, **Oxford Learner's** and **Longman** (also as apps) show it like this:
1. Type the word, e.g. *hotel*.
2. Look at the pronunciation between slashes: **/həʊˈtel/**. You don't need to read every symbol.
3. Find the small **high** mark **ˈ**. The syllable **right after it** is stressed: /həʊ**ˈtel**/ = ho-TEL. The dots (.) show where syllables split: /ˈtiː.tʃər/ = TEA-cher.
4. Press the **speaker** button (UK or US), listen, and copy.

**Two things that can confuse you:**
- Some long words also have a small **low** mark **ˌ**, like *fifteen* /ˌfɪfˈtiːn/. That's a weaker stress: ignore it for now and look for the **high** mark.
- Not every dictionary uses the same system. Some put the mark **after** the syllable, and some print the strong syllable in **bold**. Check the guide at the front of your dictionary. Cambridge, Oxford and Longman all put ˈ **before** it.

id.text:
Tidak yakin di mana tekanannya? Kamus bahasa Inggris yang bagus memberi tahu. Kamus online gratis seperti **Cambridge**, **Oxford Learner's** dan **Longman** (juga ada aplikasinya) menunjukkannya seperti ini:
1. Ketik katanya, misalnya *hotel*.
2. Lihat cara bacanya di antara dua garis miring: **/həʊˈtel/**. Kamu tidak perlu bisa membaca semua simbolnya.
3. Cari tanda kecil di **atas** **ˈ**. Suku kata **tepat sesudahnya** yang ditekan: /həʊ**ˈtel**/ = ho-TEL. Titik (.) menunjukkan batas suku kata: /ˈtiː.tʃər/ = TEA-cher.
4. Tekan tombol **speaker** (UK atau US), dengarkan, lalu tirukan.

**Dua hal yang bisa membingungkan:**
- Beberapa kata panjang juga punya tanda kecil di **bawah** **ˌ**, seperti *fifteen* /ˌfɪfˈtiːn/. Itu tekanan yang lebih lemah: abaikan dulu dan cari tanda yang di **atas**.
- Tidak semua kamus memakai sistem yang sama. Ada yang menaruh tanda **sesudah** suku kata, ada yang mencetak suku kata kuatnya dengan huruf **tebal**. Cek petunjuk di bagian depan kamusmu. Cambridge, Oxford dan Longman semuanya menaruh ˈ **sebelum** suku kata itu.

id.note: abaikan ˌ yang di bawah → In-do-NE-sia

blocks.text: Make it a habit: every time you learn a new word, check its stress and press the speaker once. It takes ten seconds and saves you from learning it wrong.

id.text: Jadikan kebiasaan: setiap kali belajar kata baru, cek tekanannya dan tekan tombol speaker sekali. Cuma sepuluh detik, dan kamu tidak akan menghafal pengucapan yang salah.

blocks.prompt: A dictionary shows fifteen /ˌfɪfˈtiːn/. Where is the main stress?
blocks.explain: The high mark ˈ is before 'tiːn', so the main stress is fif-TEEN. The low mark ˌ at the start is only a weaker stress.

id.prompt: Kamus menunjukkan fifteen /ˌfɪfˈtiːn/. Di mana tekanan utamanya?
id.explain: Tanda atas ˈ ada sebelum 'tiːn', jadi tekanan utamanya fif-TEEN. Tanda bawah ˌ di awal hanya tekanan yang lebih lemah.

id.intro: Hari ini kamu belajar membuat satu bagian kata jadi kuat, seperti TEA-cher dan ho-TEL, dan menyelesaikan kata yang berakhir dua konsonan, seperti desk dan lunch. Kamu juga belajar mencari tekanan kata apa pun di kamus. Dengarkan, tirukan, dan ucapkan setiap kata dengan suara keras!
